claims.text: The starting material is nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11.
Nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 can be prepared by conventional methods suitable for bulk fabrication.
The intervention is addition of approximately 0.5 wt% nanoscale Y2O3 during processing.
Processing will produce a uniform dispersion of Y2O3 nanoparticles at grain boundaries and within grains.
Y2O3 particles will provide preferential sites for recombination of irradiation defects.
Y2O3 particles will act as sinks for radiation-induced point defects.
The Y2O3 particles will act as heterogeneous nucleation sites while preventing radiation-induced precipitation.
Absorption of point defects by Y2O3 will reduce the thermodynamic driving force for homogeneous radiation-induced precipitation.
Defect absorption by Y2O3 will mitigate irradiation-induced solute clustering.
Unmodified nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 exhibits negligible irradiation hardening under the relevant irradiation conditions.
At approximately 8 dpa and 700–900 °C, the Y2O3-modified alloy will have about 50% less radiation-induced precipitate volume fraction than the unmodified alloy.
Y2O3 addition will not significantly increase irradiation hardening relative to the unmodified alloy.
Y2O3 addition will maintain or enhance performance under fusion-relevant irradiation.
The proposed mechanism and outcomes apply for energetic-particle irradiation up to about 8 dpa at 700–900 °C.
The applicability of the hypothesis assumes that Y2O3 does not adversely affect bulk fabrication.
Y2O3 nanoparticles may fail to disperse uniformly or remain stable during high-temperature bulk fabrication.
Y2O3 nanoparticles may nucleate other deleterious phases during irradiation.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis says the intervention will prevent radiation-induced precipitation, implying elimination, whereas the quantitative prediction is only an approximately 50% reduction in precipitate volume fraction.
